pages.title: Unit 3B: Applications of Integration
Area Between Curves
Choosing Vertical or Horizontal Slices
Volumes by Slicing
pages.body_latex:
\section{Volumes by Slicing}
\lessonobjective{Model volume as the integral of cross-sectional area.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={A solid is accumulated cross-sectional area}]
If we know the area of a cross-section at each position, a thin slab has volume approximately equal to cross-sectional area times thickness. Summing the slabs and taking a limit gives \(V=\int A(x)\,dx\) or \(V=\int A(y)\,dy\). This principle covers far more than solids of revolution: squares, triangles, semicircles, and other prescribed shapes all fit the same model.

The essential modeling step is translating a length in the base region into the dimension of the cross-section. State whether that length is a side, diameter, radius, base, or height before writing \(A(x)\). Units provide a useful check: area units times length units must produce cubic units. If the integrand does not have units of volume per unit input, the geometry has probably been mistranslated.
\end{bgexposition}


If a solid has cross-sectional area \(A(x)\) perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis, then
\[
V=\int_a^bA(x)\,dx.
\]
A thin slab has approximate volume \(A(x_i^*)\Delta x\). The integral adds the slabs in the limit.

\begin{bgapplication}[title={A wedge with triangular cross-sections}]
A solid has base \(0\le x\le4\), and the cross-section at \(x\) is an equilateral triangle with side \(s(x)=\sqrt{x}\). Since triangle area is \(\sqrt3s^2/4\),
\[
A(x)=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}x,
\qquad
V=\int_0^4\frac{\sqrt3}{4}x\,dx=2\sqrt3.
\]
\end{bgapplication}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3b-slicing-01}{rational}{8/3}[Quick check]
A solid has square cross-sections of side \(x\) for \(0\le x\le2\). Find its volume.
\begin{bghint}Cross-sectional area is \(x^2\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[\int_0^2x^2\,dx=\frac{8}{3}.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Disks and Washers
Cylindrical Shells
pages.body_latex:
\section{Cylindrical Shells}
\lessonobjective{Use radius-times-height shell formulas and choose shells when they simplify the geometry.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Shells accumulate thin cylindrical walls}]
A strip parallel to the axis of rotation sweeps out a thin cylindrical shell. Its volume is approximately circumference times height times thickness: \(2\pi(\text{radius})(\text{height})(\text{thickness})\). The radius is the strip's distance from the axis, while the height is the length of the strip inside the region.

Shells are especially useful when washers would require solving for the other variable or splitting the region. They preserve the original orientation of many function descriptions. As with every volume method, draw one strip and imagine its rotation. If the strip is parallel to the axis, shells are natural; if it is perpendicular, disks or washers are natural. That geometric distinction is more reliable than memorizing which formula uses \(dx\).
\end{bgexposition}


A thin cylindrical shell has approximate volume
\[
2\pi(\text{radius})(\text{height})(\text{thickness}).
\]
Thus
\[
V=2\pi\int_a^b r(x)h(x)\,dx.
\]

\begin{bgexample}[title={Rotate under a parabola around the y-axis}]
Rotate the region under \(y=4-x^2\) above the \(x\)-axis for \(0\le x\le2\) about the \(y\)-axis. Shell radius is \(x\), height is \(4-x^2\):
\[
V=2\pi\int_0^2x(4-x^2)dx=8\pi.
\]
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3b-shell-01}{expression}{8pi}[Quick check]
Use shells to rotate the region under \(y=4-x^2\), \(0\le x\le2\), about the y-axis.
\begin{bghint}Radius is \(x\), height is \(4-x^2\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[2\pi\int_0^2x(4-x^2)dx=8\pi.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Choosing a Volume Method
Arc Length
pages.body_latex:
\section{Arc Length}
\lessonobjective{Derive and apply the arc-length formula for graphs in x or y.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Curved length is a limit of straight lengths}]
To measure a curve, approximate it by many short line segments. Each segment is the hypotenuse of a tiny right triangle with horizontal change \(\Delta x\) and vertical change \(\Delta y\). The Pythagorean theorem gives the segment length, and the derivative replaces the ratio \(\Delta y/\Delta x\) in the limiting process. This produces the arc-length factor \(\sqrt{1+[f'(x)]^2}\).

Arc-length integrals are often harder to evaluate than they are to set up. The square root may not simplify to an elementary antiderivative, so a numerical answer can be the appropriate final result. Distinguish setup from evaluation: a correct exact integral already represents the length. Check the special case of a straight line, where the formula should agree with the ordinary distance formula.
\end{bgexposition}


A short piece of curve behaves approximately like the hypotenuse of a tiny right triangle:
\[
\Delta s\approx\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}.
\]
Dividing by \(\Delta x\) and passing to the limit gives
\[
L=\int_a^b\sqrt{1+[f'(x)]^2}\,dx.
\]

\begin{bgexample}[title={Length of a straight line}]
For \(f(x)=2x+1\) on \([0,3]\), \(f'=2\), so
\[
L=\int_0^3\sqrt5\,dx=3\sqrt5.
\]
This matches the distance formula between \((0,1)\) and \((3,7)\).
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3b-arc-01}{expression}{3sqrt(5)}[Quick check]
Find the arc length of \(y=2x+1\) on \([0,3]\).
\begin{bghint}The derivative is constant 2.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[L=\int_0^3\sqrt{1+4}\,dx=3\sqrt5.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Surface Area of Revolution
Density and Mass
Moments and Center of Mass
pages.body_latex:
\section{Moments and Center of Mass}
\lessonobjective{Compute the first moment and center of mass of a one-dimensional object.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Center of mass is a weighted average of position}]
A center of mass is not generally the geometric midpoint. Pieces with more mass exert more influence on the balance point. The moment about an origin multiplies each small mass contribution by its position, and integrating produces the total weighted position. Dividing the moment by total mass gives the center of mass.

The choice of origin affects the moment but not the physical balance point after the coordinates are interpreted consistently. Symmetry can simplify calculations and should be used before integration. A sensible final answer must lie within the object's occupied interval or region. If it falls outside, either the moment sign, density, or total mass has been mishandled.
\end{bgexposition}


For density \(\lambda(x)\), mass is
\[
m=\int_a^b\lambda(x)dx,
\]
and the moment about the origin is
\[
M=\int_a^bx\lambda(x)dx.
\]
The center of mass is
\[
\bar{x}=\frac{M}{m}.
\]

\begin{bgexample}[title={Center of mass of the increasing-density rod}]
For \(\lambda(x)=2+x\) on \([0,3]\),
\[
m=\frac{21}{2},
\qquad
M=\int_0^3x(2+x)dx=18.
\]
Thus
\[
\bar{x}=\frac{18}{21/2}=\frac{12}{7}\text{ m}.
\]
This lies to the right of the midpoint \(1.5\), as expected because density increases with \(x\).
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3b-com-01}{rational}{12/7}[Quick check]
For density \(\lambda(x)=2+x\) on \([0,3]\), find the center of mass.
\begin{bghint}Compute mass and moment, then divide.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[\bar{x}=18/(21/2)=12/7.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Work and Variable Force
Work Done on Springs
Pumping Liquids
pages.body_latex:
\section{Pumping Liquids}
\lessonobjective{Build work integrals from slice volume, fluid weight density, and lifting distance.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Every fluid layer travels a different distance}]
Pumping problems combine three local quantities: the volume of a thin fluid slice, its weight per unit volume, and the distance that slice must be lifted. A horizontal slice at height \(y\) has volume approximately \(A(y)dy\), weight approximately \(\gamma A(y)dy\), and work approximately weight times lifting distance. Integrating over the fluid depth adds the work for all slices.

The lifting distance is often the most commonly omitted factor. It must be measured from the slice's current height to the outlet, not from the bottom of the tank unless those distances happen to coincide. A sketch with the coordinate axis, fluid level, slice, and outlet labeled is essential. The resulting integrand should have units of energy per unit height before multiplication by \(dy\).
\end{bgexposition}


For a horizontal slice at height \(y\):
\[
\text{slice volume}=A(y)\,dy,
\]
\[
\text{slice weight}=\delta A(y)\,dy,
\]
where \(\delta\) is weight density, and
\[
dW=\delta A(y)D(y)\,dy.
\]

\begin{bgapplication}[title={Pump water from a rectangular tank}]
A tank is 4 m long, 3 m wide, and 2 m deep, filled with water. Pump water to an outlet 1 m above the top. Let \(y\) measure height from the bottom. Cross-sectional area is \(12\), lift distance is \(3-y\), and water weight density is approximately \(9800\) N/m\(^3\):
\[
W=9800\int_0^2 12(3-y)dy.
\]
The setup is the main modeling achievement; evaluation is routine.
\end{bgapplication}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3b-pump-01}{expression}{117600*integral_0^2(3-y)dy}[Quick check]
For the rectangular water tank described in the lesson, write the work integral.
\begin{bghint}Use weight density times cross-sectional area times lifting distance.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[W=9800\int_0^2 12(3-y)dy.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Fluid Pressure and Hydrostatic Force
pages.body_latex:
\section{Fluid Pressure and Hydrostatic Force}
\lessonobjective{Integrate pressure over a submerged surface using horizontal strips.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Pressure depends on depth, force also depends on area}]
Fluid pressure increases linearly with depth according to \(p=\gamma h\), where \(\gamma\) is weight density. Pressure alone is not force. A thin strip of a submerged plate experiences force approximately equal to pressure at that depth times the strip's area. Integrating these strip forces gives the total hydrostatic force.

The depth variable and strip width depend on the geometry and coordinate choice. A strip near the surface has lower pressure than an equally sized strip deeper down. For vertical plates, horizontal strips usually keep depth constant across each strip and are therefore natural. Check that pressure units multiplied by area units produce force units, and distinguish depth below the surface from height above the bottom.
\end{bgexposition}


Fluid pressure at depth \(h\) is
\[
p=\delta h,
\]
where \(\delta\) is weight density. A horizontal strip of width \(w(y)\) and thickness \(dy\) has area \(w(y)dy\), so
\[
dF=\delta h(y)w(y)dy.
\]

\begin{bgapplication}[title={A rectangular gate}]
A vertical rectangular gate is 2 m wide and extends from the water surface to depth 3 m. With \(y\) measured downward,
\[
F=9800\int_0^3 y(2)dy=88200\text{ N}.
\]
\end{bgapplication}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3b-fluid-01}{integer}{88200}[Quick check]
A 2 m wide rectangular gate extends from the water surface to depth 3 m. Use water weight density \(9800\,\mathrm{N/m^3}\). Find the total force.
\begin{bghint}Integrate \(9800\cdot y\cdot2\) from 0 to 3.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[19600[y^2/2]_0^3=88200\text{ N}.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Recovering Totals from Marginal Quantities
pages.body_latex:
\section{Recovering Totals from Marginal Quantities}
\lessonobjective{Integrate marginal cost, revenue, or profit to recover total change.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={A marginal function is a rate of total change}]
In economics, a marginal quantity is a derivative. Marginal cost \(C'(q)\) measures the approximate change in total cost for one additional unit near production level \(q\). Integrating a marginal function over a production interval recovers the net change in the corresponding total function. One known total value is then needed to recover the absolute total.

The interpretation should not be reduced to symbol manipulation. The integral \(\int_a^b C'(q)\,dq\) is the increase in cost from producing \(a\) units to producing \(b\) units, not the total cost at \(b\) unless \(C(a)=0\). Units provide the distinction: dollars per unit times units gives dollars. The same reasoning applies to marginal revenue, marginal profit, and other accumulated business quantities.
\end{bgexposition}


If \(C'(q)\) is marginal cost in dollars per unit, then the added cost of increasing production from \(q=a\) to \(q=b\) is
\[
C(b)-C(a)=\int_a^bC'(q)dq.
\]
An initial fixed cost determines the constant when a complete cost function is required.

\begin{bgapplication}[title={Production expansion}]
Suppose \(C'(q)=20+0.04q\) dollars per item and \(C(0)=5000\). Then
\[
C(q)=20q+0.02q^2+5000.
\]
The cost of expanding production from 100 to 150 items is
\[
\int_{100}^{150}(20+0.04q)dq.
\]
\end{bgapplication}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3b-marginal-01}{integer}{2600}[Quick check]
If \(C'(q)=20+0.04q\), find the added cost from \(q=100\) to \(q=200\).
\begin{bghint}Integrate marginal cost over the production interval.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[\bigl[20q+0.02q^2\bigr]_{100}^{200}=2600.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Probability Density and Expected Value
pages.body_latex:
\section{Probability Density and Expected Value}
\lessonobjective{Interpret probability as accumulated density and calculate expected value for a continuous model.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Probability is continuous mass distributed over outcomes}]
For a continuous random variable, a density function does not give the probability of one exact value. Probabilities come from integrating density over intervals. The total area under a valid density must equal one, and the density must be nonnegative. Thus \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) measures the probability that the random variable falls between \(a\) and \(b\).

Expected value is a weighted average in which each possible value is weighted by its density. The integral \(E[X]=\int x f(x)\,dx\) is therefore closely related to center of mass. A density may be greater than one at some points without violating probability rules; only integrated probability must lie between zero and one. Always verify normalization before using a proposed function as a probability density.
\end{bgexposition}


A probability density \(p(x)\) satisfies \(p(x)\ge0\) and
\[
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}p(x)dx=1.
\]
Probabilities are areas:
\[
P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^bp(x)dx.
\]
The expected value is
\[
E[X]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}xp(x)dx,
\]
when the improper integral converges.

\begin{bgexample}[title={A simple triangular density}]
Let \(p(x)=2x\) on \([0,1]\) and \(0\) elsewhere. It is normalized because
\[
\int_0^12x\,dx=1.
\]
Then
\[
P(X\le1/2)=\int_0^{1/2}2x\,dx=\frac14,
\]
and
\[
E[X]=\int_0^1x(2x)dx=\frac23.
\]
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{u3b-prob-01}{rational}{1/4}[Quick check]
For density \(p(x)=2x\) on \([0,1]\), find \(P(X\le1/2)\).
\begin{bghint}Integrate the density from 0 to 1/2.\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}\[[x^2]_0^{1/2}=1/4.\]\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

pages.title: Physics Application Studio
Unit 3B Review: Applications of Integration
pages.body_latex:
\section{Unit 3B Review}
\begin{bgsummary}[title={Modeling questions to ask}]
\begin{enumerate}
\item What small object or contribution am I adding?
\item What variable naturally locates that object?
\item What is its size, density, force, or distance factor?
\item What are the correct bounds?
\item Do the units of the integrand times the differential produce the desired units?
\item Does the sign have physical or geometric meaning?
\end{enumerate}
\end{bgsummary}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item Find an area between two curves using vertical slices.
\item Set up the same area using horizontal slices.
\item Compute a washer volume and shell volume for one region and compare.
\item Find volume with semicircular cross-sections.
\item Find arc length of a linear function and explain agreement with geometry.
\item Compute mass and center of mass of a nonuniform rod.
\item Calculate work for a spring.
\item Set up pumping work for a conical tank.
\item Compute force on a submerged rectangular plate.
\item Recover total cost from marginal cost.
\end{bgexercises}

pages.title: Common Application Errors and How to Repair Them
pages.body_latex:
\section{Common Application Errors}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Writing an integral before drawing a representative slice.
\item Using top-minus-bottom with a horizontal slice.
\item Measuring a radius from the wrong axis.
\item Forgetting to square disk and washer radii.
\item Using shell height as a radius.
\item Omitting the arc-length factor in surface area.
\item Mixing mass density and weight density.
\item Using constant-force work when force varies.
\item Treating pressure as total force rather than force per area.
\item Reporting a number without units or contextual meaning.
\end{enumerate}

pages.title: Unit 3B Cumulative Practice
pages.body_latex:
\section{Cumulative Practice}
\begin{bgexercises}
\item Find the area enclosed by \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x+3\).
\item Rotate a bounded region around a horizontal line using washers.
\item Rotate the same region around a vertical line using shells.
\item Find the volume of a solid with square cross-sections.
\item Find the arc length of \(y=x^{3/2}\) on a short interval where the integral is manageable.
\item Find the mass and center of mass of a rod with density \(1+x^2\).
\item Find work to stretch a calibrated spring from one nonzero extension to another.
\item Set up work to pump liquid from a triangular trough.
\item Find hydrostatic force on a triangular gate.
\item Recover a cost function from marginal cost and fixed cost.
\item Normalize a simple probability density and compute its expected value.
\end{bgexercises}

pages.title: Unit 3B Practice Exam A
pages.body_latex:
\section{Practice Exam A}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Find the area between \(y=2x\) and \(y=x^2\) on \([0,2]\).
\item The region bounded by \(x=y^2\) and \(x=y+2\) is described most naturally with horizontal slices. Find its area.
\item Rotate the region under \(y=\sqrt{x}\), \(0\le x\le4\), around the \(x\)-axis. Find the volume.
\item Use cylindrical shells to rotate the region under \(y=4-x^2\), \(0\le x\le2\), around the \(y\)-axis.
\item A solid has square cross-sections perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis. The side length is \(2-x\) for \(0\le x\le2\). Find the volume.
\item Find the arc length of \(y=2x+1\) on \([0,3]\).
\item A rod occupies \([0,3]\) and has density \(\lambda(x)=2+x\) kg/m. Find its mass and center of mass.
\item A force \(F(x)=10+3x\) newtons moves an object from \(x=0\) to \(x=4\) meters. Find the work.
\item A rectangular tank is 4 m long, 3 m wide, and 2 m deep, and is full of water. Water is pumped to an outlet 1 m above the top. Set up and evaluate the work using water weight density \(9800\,\mathrm{N/m^3}\).
\item A vertical rectangular gate is 2 m wide and extends from the water surface to a depth of 3 m. Find the hydrostatic force using water weight density \(9800\,\mathrm{N/m^3}\).
\item If marginal cost is \(C'(q)=20+0.04q\), find the added cost of increasing production from 100 to 200 units.
\item The probability density is \(p(x)=2x\) on \([0,1]\). Find \(P(X\le1/2)\) and \(E[X]\).
\item For one problem above, explain how the units of the slice contribution become the units of the final answer. Also give one independent reasonableness check.
\end{enumerate}

pages.title: Unit 3B Practice Exam A Answer Key
pages.body_latex:
\section{Practice Exam A Answer Key}
For modeling problems, full credit requires a correct representative slice or contribution, bounds, units, and interpretation.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
\[
A=\int_0^2(2x-x^2)dx=\frac43.
\]
\item Intersections are \(y=-1,2\), and the line is to the right:
\[
A=\int_{-1}^{2}\bigl[(y+2)-y^2\bigr]dy=\frac92.
\]
\item
\[
V=\pi\int_0^4(\sqrt{x})^2dx=8\pi.
\]
\item
\[
V=2\pi\int_0^2x(4-x^2)dx=8\pi.
\]
\item
\[
V=\int_0^2(2-x)^2dx=\frac83.
\]
\item
\[
L=\int_0^3\sqrt{1+2^2}\,dx=3\sqrt5.
\]
\item
\[
m=\int_0^3(2+x)dx=\frac{21}{2},
\qquad
\bar x=\frac{\int_0^3x(2+x)dx}{m}=\frac{12}{7}\text{ m}.
\]
\item
\[
W=\int_0^4(10+3x)dx=64\text{ J}.
\]
\item Let \(y\) measure height above the bottom. A slice has volume \(12dy\), weight \(9800(12)dy\), and lifting distance \(3-y\):
\[
W=117600\int_0^2(3-y)dy=470400\text{ J}.
\]
\item
\[
F=9800\int_0^3 2y\,dy=88200\text{ N}.
\]
\item
\[
\int_{100}^{200}(20+0.04q)dq=2600\text{ dollars}.
\]
\item
\[
P(X\le1/2)=\int_0^{1/2}2x\,dx=\frac14,
\qquad
E[X]=\int_0^1x(2x)dx=\frac23.
\]
\item A correct response identifies, for example, \((\mathrm{N/m^3})(\mathrm{m^3})(\mathrm{m})=\mathrm{N\,m}=\mathrm{J}\) in a pumping problem. A reasonableness check may use sign, units, comparison with a constant-force estimate, geometric bounds, or expected magnitude.
\end{enumerate}

pages.title: Unit 3B Practice Exam B
pages.body_latex:
\section{Practice Exam B}
\begin{enumerate}
\item Find the area enclosed by \(y=x+2\) and \(y=x^2\).
\item Rotate the region under \(y=1-x^2\), \(0\le x\le1\), around the \(x\)-axis. Find the volume.
\item Rotate the same region around the \(y\)-axis using cylindrical shells.
\item A solid has semicircular cross-sections perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis. The diameter at \(x\) is \(2\sqrt{x}\) for \(0\le x\le4\). Find the volume.
\item Find the surface area generated by rotating \(y=x\), \(0\le x\le1\), around the \(x\)-axis.
\item A rod occupies \([0,1]\) and has density \(\lambda(x)=1+x^2\). Find its mass and center of mass.
\item A spring has constant \(k=200\,\mathrm{N/m}\). Find the work required to stretch it from 0.10 m to 0.30 m beyond equilibrium.
\item A vertical cylindrical tank has radius 1 m and height 2 m and is full of water. Pump the water to an outlet 1 m above the top. Set up and evaluate the work.
\item A triangular gate has its top edge at the water surface, width 4 m at the surface, and vertex 3 m below the surface. Find the hydrostatic force.
\item If \(C'(q)=15+0.02q\) and \(C(0)=2000\), find \(C(300)\).
\item The density \(p(x)=3x^2\) is defined on \([0,1]\). Verify normalization and find \(E[X]\).
\item For the region under \(y=1-x^2\) on \([0,1]\), explain why shells are natural about the \(y\)-axis while disks are natural about the \(x\)-axis.
\item Critique this statement: ``Once an integral is written, units and geometry no longer matter.'' Give at least two concrete reasons it is false.
\end{enumerate}

pages.title: Unit 3B Practice Exam B Answer Key
pages.body_latex:
\section{Practice Exam B Answer Key}
For modeling problems, full credit requires the local contribution, bounds, units, and an interpreted result.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Intersections are \(x=-1,2\):
\[
A=\int_{-1}^{2}(x+2-x^2)dx=\frac92.
\]
\item
\[
V=\pi\int_0^1(1-x^2)^2dx=\frac{8\pi}{15}.
\]
\item
\[
V=2\pi\int_0^1x(1-x^2)dx=\frac{\pi}{2}.
\]
\item The area of a semicircle with diameter \(d\) is \(\pi d^2/8\), so
\[
V=\int_0^4\frac{\pi(2\sqrt{x})^2}{8}dx=4\pi.
\]
\item
\[
S=2\pi\int_0^1x\sqrt{1+1^2}dx=\pi\sqrt2.
\]
\item
\[
m=\int_0^1(1+x^2)dx=\frac43,
\qquad
\bar x=\frac{\int_0^1x(1+x^2)dx}{m}=\frac{9}{16}.
\]
\item
\[
W=\int_{0.10}^{0.30}200x\,dx=8\text{ J}.
\]
\item With \(y\) measured from the bottom, slice volume is \(\pi dy\) and lift distance is \(3-y\):
\[
W=9800\pi\int_0^2(3-y)dy=39200\pi\text{ J}.
\]
\item Let \(y\) be depth below the surface. The width is \(4(1-y/3)\):
\[
F=9800\int_0^3 y\,4\left(1-\frac y3\right)dy=58800\text{ N}.
\]
\item
\[
C(300)=2000+\int_0^{300}(15+0.02q)dq=7400.
\]
\item
\[
\int_0^1 3x^2dx=1,
\qquad
E[X]=\int_0^1x(3x^2)dx=\frac34.
\]
\item Vertical strips are parallel to the \(y\)-axis and create shells around the \(y\)-axis; the same vertical strips are perpendicular to the \(x\)-axis and create disks around the \(x\)-axis. Both methods preserve the given \(x\)-description without solving for an inverse function.
\item Units verify that the local contribution has the right physical dimension, while geometry determines radii, heights, widths, and distances. Ignoring either can yield a numerically evaluated integral that represents the wrong quantity.
\end{enumerate}
